outcome.text: The question lands like a dropped plate. For a moment the whole performance is visible from the inside — the fire, the gourds, the impressive meal, all of it built nightly against a silence he cannot sit in. He does not answer. But he stops pouring, and after a while he asks you how one learns to sit still, and you tell him, and he listens.

animal_forest_gana_ceremony.title: Gana Ceremony
animal_forest_gana_ceremony.text:
The clearing is full of gana, arranged in concentric rings, and every one of them is dancing — not chaotically, but in a slow interlocking pattern that has clearly been going on for hours and shows no sign of ending.

Nobody is watching. That is not what it is for.

choices.text: Watch from the treeline

outcome.text: You stay for an hour, understanding none of it, moved anyway. When you leave nobody has acknowledged you, and it does not feel like a slight.

choices.text: Go around the clearing without disturbing it

outcome.text: You add an hour to the day's walk and disturb nothing. The drumming follows you for a long way.

choices.text: Join the outer ring

outcome.text: You step in on the beat and the ring absorbs you without breaking stride. It is harder than it looks and then, abruptly, much easier — the pattern does the thinking if you let it. Somewhere in the third hour you stop being a visitor. At dawn the eldest presses her forehead to yours and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Whatever it is for, they are glad about it. Be glad too.

outcome.text:
You do not know the steps and you join the outer ring anyway, and the outer ring is precisely where people who do not know the steps are supposed to be.

By the third round you have most of it. By the fifth you are being corrected, kindly, by a gana half your height.

choices.text: Work out what the ceremony is for

outcome.text: The rings are moving at different rates — outer fast, inner slow, the centre almost still. It is a calendar. They are dancing a year, and the still figure at the centre is the year that has ended. It is a funeral. You take your hat off and stay until it finishes.

animal_forest_rakshasa_den.title: Rakshasa Den
animal_forest_rakshasa_den.text:
The cave mouth is screened by hanging root and would be invisible from ten paces. Inside, the floor is dry sand, deliberately swept, and the walls are stacked with what a rakshasa considers worth keeping.

The den is empty. The bedding is warm.

choices.text: Leave now, quickly

outcome.text: You are a quarter-mile away before you let yourself breathe properly. It is, on reflection, the best decision you have made today.

choices.text: Take what you can and go

outcome.text: You grab from the nearest stack and are out in ninety seconds. Something calls, far off and unhurried, and you do not stop moving for an hour.

choices.text: Search it properly — the good things will be buried

outcome_success.text: Under the sand at the back, where the sweeping is most careful, there is a hollow lined with cloth. What is in it has nothing to do with hunting and everything to do with whatever this rakshasa was before it came out here to be a predator.

outcome_failure.text: You are elbow-deep in the sand at the back of the cave when the light from the entrance changes shape.

choices.text: Prepare the den before its owner returns

outcome.text: You do not steal anything. You rearrange: the bedding, the stacks, the sand, all of it shifted an inch or two out of true. Then you wait outside. The rakshasa comes home, stops dead in the entrance, and spends the next twenty minutes in a state of profound existential unease. It leaves the valley that night. You take the den at your leisure.

animal_forest_mushroom_maze.title: Mushroom Maze
animal_forest_mushroom_maze.text:
The fruiting bodies here are the size of buildings, and they have grown close enough together to make corridors. The light under them is the colour of weak tea, the air is thick with spores, and sound does not carry the way it should.

After twenty minutes you pass the same distinctively split cap for the second time.

choices.text: Retrace your steps and go around

outcome.text: It takes an unnerving amount of time to find the edge again, but you find it. The party is quiet for a while afterwards.

choices.text: Push on and trust your sense of direction

outcome_success.text: You keep the slope on your left and refuse to be argued out of it, and the corridors eventually run out of ways to disagree with you. You come out the far side having crossed in a third of the time the detour would have taken — and having gathered a great deal on the way.

outcome_failure.text: Hours. The spores get into everything, and by the end at least two of you are seeing things in the corridors that the others are not. You come out somewhere you did not intend to be, tired and rattled.

choices.text: Work the maze deliberately for what grows here

outcome.text: You stop trying to get out and start trying to get value, which turns out to be the correct relationship with the place. Half a day later you leave by the entrance you came in, loaded, having mapped the good stands by the smell of the air in each corridor.

choices.text: There is something to be heard here and you are not going to hear it.

outcome.text:
The others stop and tilt their heads and go quiet, and you watch them do it and understand only that something has been heard.

By the time it has been explained the thing that made the sound has moved, and the party's route with it.

choices.text: Nobody is getting lost in here on your watch.

outcome.text:
You mark every third turning, consistently, on the same side, at the same height.

It is fussy and slow and the party complains about it right up until the point where you walk everyone back out in a fifth of the time it took to walk in.

choices.text: Stop moving and listen to the maze

outcome.text: The corridors are not a maze. They are one organism's idea of a shape, and it is not trying to trap you — it has simply never had a reason to consider the concept of a straight line. Once you stop expecting corridors to behave like corridors, the way out is obvious, and always was.

animal_forest_banyan_hollow.title: Ancient Banyan
animal_forest_banyan_hollow.text:
The banyan has been walking for a thousand years — dropping roots, standing on them, letting the original trunk rot away — and what is left is a hollow cathedral of living wood a hundred paces across, with a floor of soft mast and a roof you cannot see.

Things have been left here. Not hidden. Left.

choices.text: Take nothing, disturb nothing

outcome.text: You walk through and out the other side. The quality of the silence stays with you for days.

choices.text: Take what has been left

outcome.text: Coins, tools, a folded cloth with something heavy inside. Nobody stops you. Nothing happens at all, which somehow makes it worse.

choices.text: Leave something of your own and take something in exchange

outcome.text: You set down coin and lift a small carved thing in its place, and the exchange feels correct in a way you could not defend to anyone. The banyan does not comment.

choices.text: Address the tree properly

outcome.text: You call, and something enormous and extremely slow turns a fraction of its attention toward you. It is not a spirit inhabiting the banyan; it is the banyan, thinking, at a speed that makes a human life look like a spark. It permits you one question. You are still deciding whether you asked the right one.

animal_forest_cliff_aerie.title: Cliff Aerie
animal_forest_cliff_aerie.text:
The nest is a cartload of branches wedged into a fissure two hundred feet up a limestone face, and it has been in continuous use for generations — the bones of a great many meals are cemented into its base by weather.

The adults are out. Something in the nest is not.

choices.text: Leave the aerie alone

outcome.text: You are a mile off when two shapes cross the sun on their way home. Good timing, you reflect.

choices.text: Climb and take what the nest has collected

outcome_success.text: Two hundred feet of limestone and then a nest full of two generations of shiny things nobody has ever come to reclaim. You are down and gone before the adults return. Your hands will not stop shaking for an hour.

outcome_failure.text: You are eighty feet up and fully committed when the shadow crosses you, and shyena do not need to land to fight.

choices.text: The chick is tangled — free it

outcome.text: It has gotten a leg through a gap in the branch weave and has been there long enough to be past panic. Freeing it takes an hour of very careful work at a height that does not bear thinking about. The adults arrive while you are doing it, and hang in the air twenty feet out, watching, and do not attack. When you finish, one of them escorts you down — pacing your descent, ledge by ledge, the whole way.

choices.text: Look at what is in the nest, not at the nest.

outcome.text:
Bone, wool, a length of dyed cord that did not come from anywhere nearby, and — under all of it — the thing the cord was tied to.

The aerie's owner has been collecting from a settlement that is not on your map, and the direction it must lie in is now obvious.

choices.text: Read the face for the updraught and go up on it

outcome.text: There is a standing column against the rock that will take a light body most of the way if it is not fought. You ride it up, take what is loose, and step off into it again on the way down. Whether the shyena saw you is unclear. If they did, they seem to have approved of the method.

animal_forest_jungle_merchant.title: Forest Merchant
animal_forest_jungle_merchant.text:
His entire stock is on his back and his back is enormous. A varaha trader, three days out from anywhere, working a circuit that he clearly holds entirely in his head.

"You're the second party this month," he says, delighted. "Business is booming."

choices.text: See what he is carrying

outcome.text: He unpacks with practiced speed, laying everything out on a groundsheet in an order that makes his own sense.

choices.text: Wish him luck and move on

outcome.text: "Tell people I'm out here!" he calls after you. "Nobody knows I'm out here!"

choices.text: Trade him route information for stock

outcome.text: You give him the state of the ridge crossings and where the shardula boundary now runs; he gives you a price no one else in this forest will ever see, and adds two items to the pile that were not for sale. Both of you leave convinced you got the better end of it, which is the mark of a good trade.

choices.text: Walk with him as far as your roads agree

outcome.text: Half a day of company. He talks the entire time — prices, gossip, a long involved grievance about a vanara bridge toll — and when your roads part he presses supplies on you and refuses payment on the grounds that conversation is worth more than goods out here.

animal_meadow_yaksha_challenge.title: Yaksha Challenge
animal_meadow_yaksha_challenge.text:
He has planted his spear in the ground across the trail and is standing beside it with his arms folded — a yaksha of considerable size and, evidently, considerable free time.

"Nobody crosses my ground without giving me something to remember them by," he announces. "Gold, a fight, or a story. Your choice. I'd prefer the fight."

choices.text: Give him the fight
Give him the gold

outcome.text: He takes it with visible disappointment and stands aside. "That's the boring one," he says. "Everyone picks the boring one."

choices.text: Give him the story

outcome.text: You tell him about the hell realms — the frost, the Warden's gate, a thing with four arms that judged souls at a doorway. He sits down halfway through and does not move again until you finish. When you do, he pulls his spear out of the ground, hands you a drinking-horn from his belt, and asks whether you would consider coming back this way.

choices.text: There is a spear in the ground across the trail.

outcome.text:
There is, and there is only one thing a spear planted across a trail has ever meant, and you have been walking all morning.

The yaksha is pleased. The bout is formal, brief, and settled on a technicality that you both agree to call a win for him.

choices.text: Accept the fight, but set the terms

outcome.text: First fall, no weapons, no grudge. He lights up like a festival. You lose — he is enormous — but you lose well enough that he hauls you up laughing and declares the toll paid twice over, then walks you to the edge of his ground telling you about every fight he has had this year.

animal_meadow_dura_patrol.title: Dura Patrol
animal_meadow_dura_patrol.text:
The ground gives slightly under your boot, and then a great deal more, and you are standing knee-deep in the roof of somebody's corridor.

Six dura come up out of the break in perfect order, mandibles first. They are not surprised. They have clearly done this exact drill many times.

choices.text: Fight clear of the breach
Withdraw slowly and let them repair it

outcome.text: You back off twenty paces and sit down, hands visible. Within the hour the breach is sealed by a work party that ignores you completely. The patrol watches you until the repair is done, then goes back down without a word.

choices.text: Help shore up the collapse

outcome.text: You cut and set a timber brace across the break before they can decide what to do about you, and the work party arrives to find the roof already held. There is a long silence. Then the patrol leader taps her mandibles twice — the dura acknowledgement — and someone brings up worked metal from below and puts it in your hands.

choices.text: Recognise the drill and stand where a friendly would

outcome.text: This is a containment formation, not an attack formation — they are protecting the corridor, not hunting you. You move to the position a dura auxiliary would take on the flank and simply hold it. The whole patrol relaxes at once. You are, briefly and administratively, part of the colony.

animal_meadow_khadga_charge.title: Khadga Charge
animal_meadow_khadga_charge.text:
The grass ahead is flattened in a long straight line, and at the far end of it a khadga is turning around.

There is no cover between you and it. There is no cover behind you either. It lowers its head.

choices.text: Stand and meet the charge
Scatter — it can only follow one of you

outcome.text: The party breaks in five directions. It commits to one, misses, ploughs a hundred paces of grass, and by the time it has turned everyone is somewhere else. You regroup a mile on, minus one pack and most of your composure.

choices.text: Hold until the last moment, then step off the line

outcome_success.text: You wait until you can see the individual hairs on its horn and then take one long pace left. It goes past close enough to knock you flat with the wind of it, and keeps going, because that is what a committed khadga does.

outcome_failure.text: You step the wrong way. It adjusts. They can adjust, it turns out, right at the end.

choices.text: You will not need to hold until the last moment. You are faster than the last moment.

outcome.text:
You step off the line with time to spare, and having time to spare means you can watch the whole thing go past from a yard away, which almost nobody gets to do.

It is enormous. You will be describing it for weeks.

choices.text: You are already running and it has not started yet.

outcome.text:
You are, and the running is the problem — a khadga follows movement, and you have supplied the only movement on the plain.

It follows you a long way before losing interest. The party finds you eventually.

choices.text: Do not move at all

outcome.text: A khadga charges movement. You stop being movement. It comes to a halt six feet away, snorting, genuinely confused, and stands there for a full minute trying to resolve you into something worth hitting. Then it wanders off to eat. The rest of the party unfreezes considerably later than you do.

animal_meadow_bhramara_swarm.title: Bhramara Swarm
animal_meadow_bhramara_swarm.text:
The sound arrives before anything else — a low chord in three parts, coming from a shadow on the grass that is moving against the wind.

The swarm is perhaps four thousand strong. It has noticed you. The chord changes key.

choices.text: Fight the swarm
Burn damp grass and go through the smoke

outcome.text: Smoke makes them sluggish and, more importantly, makes the chord fall apart — a swarm that cannot hear itself is just a lot of individual insects. You walk out through the confusion, coughing.

choices.text: Answer the chord

outcome.text: You find the root note and hold it, and then the fifth, and the swarm — which is a single distributed mind conducting a conversation with itself — abruptly has something else to talk to. The chord resolves into something almost welcoming. They escort you across their range in a loose column and peel away at the boundary, still singing.

choices.text: Do not run from a swarm. Nobody has ever outrun one.

outcome.text:
You stop, and you make everyone else stop, which is much harder.

The chord passes over and around and does not descend, because nothing in the party is behaving like something worth descending on.

choices.text: Break the swarm's formation with moving air

outcome.text: You put a shear across their line of advance. The swarm is not hurt — it is *edited*, the coherent shape torn into six shapes that have to spend the next several minutes deciding which of them is in charge. You are long gone before they settle it.

animal_meadow_patanga_ascetic.title: Patanga Ascetic
animal_meadow_patanga_ascetic.text:
He is standing in the open with his wings fully spread, facing directly into the sun, and has evidently been doing so since it rose. The grass around him is scorched in a perfect circle.

"Don't stand in front," he says pleasantly. "You'll shade me."

choices.text: Step out of his light and go

outcome.text: "Thank you," he says, without moving. "Very few people think of it."

choices.text: Ask what the practice is for

outcome.text: "To want the fire and not enter it. Anyone can burn. Standing at the edge is the discipline." He has been at it, he mentions, for eleven years. His wings are scarred to lace.

choices.text: Stand with him until sundown

outcome.text: Nine hours. The heat is unspeakable and the boredom is worse and somewhere in the seventh hour the two stop being different from each other. At sundown he folds his wings and looks at you for the first time. "You wanted to leave at the fourth hour," he says. "You stayed. That is the whole teaching. There is nothing else."

choices.text: You know what he is doing. Stand in it with him.

outcome.text:
Wings spread, in the open, in full sun, until sundown. It is a stupid practice and you both know it is a stupid practice and that is not an argument against it.

When the light goes he folds his wings and says one sentence to you, and it is not about the practice.

choices.text: You have already given up more than a day of sun.

outcome.text:
You stand past sundown, which he does not, and he comes back at moonrise to find out what you are doing.

The conversation that follows is the first one in months in which neither of you has to explain the premise.

choices.text: Argue that the discipline is just a slower burning

outcome.text: You put it to him: that standing at the edge for eleven years is not restraint but an extended indulgence, the wanting kept alive deliberately because he is afraid of what he would be without it. He is silent for a very long time. Then: "Yes." Just that. He folds his wings and walks away north, and you never learn where he goes.

animal_meadow_yaksha_shaman.title: Yaksha Shaman
animal_meadow_yaksha_shaman.text:
She has laid out a divination on a hide: knucklebones, seed-pods, a scatter of bright beetle-wings, all of it arranged in a pattern that is clearly precise and entirely opaque.

"Sit down," she says. "You're in it. You've been in it since yesterday."

choices.text: You would rather not know

outcome.text: "Sensible," she says, and sweeps the beetle-wings into her palm. "Most of it is weather anyway."

choices.text: Sit down and hear it

outcome.text: She tells you three things. One is about the road north and is immediately useful. One is about somebody in your party and you decide not to repeat it. The third she will not explain at all — "It hasn't got a shape yet" — but she writes it on a scrap of bark and makes you take it.

choices.text: Read the pattern alongside her

outcome.text: You know a different system, but the grammar is the same, and for an hour the two of you argue happily about correspondences like colleagues at a conference. She teaches you her reading of the beetle-wings; you show her something about the seed-pods that genuinely surprises her. She insists on gifting you her spare set.

choices.text: Watch her hands, not the bones.

outcome.text:
The bones land where she puts them. That is not a fraud — she is not pretending otherwise, and when she sees you watching her hands she nods as though a question has been settled.

What she tells you afterwards, without the bones, is the useful part.

choices.text: Ask her what she can see of where you are going after this life

outcome.text: She looks for a long time. Then she gathers the bones up without answering and says, gently: "It is not fixed. That is the good news, and it is also the only news." You get the distinct impression she saw something and chose kindness over accuracy — and that she was right to.

animal_meadow_dura_artisan.title: Dura Artisan
animal_meadow_dura_artisan.text:
The surface entrance to the warren has been decorated — and not modestly. Somebody has spent years carving the entire rim into an interlocking relief of the colony's history, and is currently, delicately, adding to it.

"Careful of the edge," she says. "It's wet."

choices.text: Admire the work and say so

outcome.text: She is entirely unembarrassed by praise and walks you through forty years of colony politics rendered in bas-relief, including two wars, a schism, and a section she describes flatly as "the mistake".

choices.text: Commission a piece

outcome.text: She takes your measure — literally, with a length of knotted cord — and produces a small carved token in under an hour. It is a likeness. It is uncomfortably good.

choices.text: Ask to add a panel of your own

outcome.text: She hands you a chisel and a corner of blank rim and does not offer advice, which is the highest compliment available. You carve the hell-gate: frost, the four-armed judge, the door. When you finish she studies it for a long while and then cuts her own mark beside yours — colony work, permanent, load-bearing history. Some dura in two hundred years will wonder who you were.

choices.text: Look at the work rather than the doorway.

outcome.text:
It is very good work. It is also, you notice, made from about nine different things that do not occur within a hundred miles of here.

You say so. The artisan is delighted — nobody has ever recognised the sourcing before, only the arrangement.

choices.text: Read "the mistake" panel carefully

outcome.text: The colony sealed a corridor with a work party still inside it, to stop a flood, and saved nine hundred lives. The panel does not editorialise; it simply records, in the same careful hand as everything else, each of the forty-one names. "We carve it so nobody has to argue about whether it happened," she says. "Only about whether it was right."

animal_meadow_cliff_oracle.title: Cliff Oracle
animal_meadow_cliff_oracle.text:
The uluka is upside down in the mouth of a cliff hollow, wings folded, eyes closed, and has been described to you by three separate strangers as the only honest oracle in the meadow.

"I only answer questions people don't want answered," she says, without opening her eyes. "It saves everyone's time."

choices.text: Leave her hanging

outcome.text: "Wise," she says. It does not sound entirely like a compliment.

choices.text: Ask something practical anyway

outcome.text: She sighs, opens one eye, and answers your dull question about the northern route accurately and at length, with the air of a scholar asked to fetch tea. The information is excellent. She is visibly disappointed in you.

choices.text: Ask the one you have been avoiding

outcome.text: Both eyes open. She listens to the whole question, including the part you did not mean to say out loud, and then answers it in one sentence that you will be turning over for months. It is not comforting. It is, unmistakably, true.

choices.text: An upside-down owl in a cliff. Ask the question properly.

outcome.text:
There is a way of asking, and you know it, because you have always known these things without being able to say where from.

The uluka answers the question you asked rather than the one you meant, which is the risk you accepted by asking properly.

choices.text: Offer her an omen of your own in trade

outcome.text: You show her the death you have been carrying since the last realm — the shape of it, not the fact. Uluka trade in ill omens the way other people trade in grain, and this is good stock. She takes it off you, which is a service you did not know you needed, and pays for it besides.

animal_meadow_dura_warren.title: Dura Warren
animal_meadow_dura_warren.text:
The entrance slopes down out of the sunlight into a corridor that is perfectly round, perfectly smooth, and perfectly dark. Warm air comes up out of it smelling of earth and formic acid.

Somewhere below, a great many things are working.

choices.text: Not today

outcome.text: The warm air follows you for the first hundred paces, like a held breath.

choices.text: Explore only the upper galleries

outcome.text: Storage. Rank on rank of it, meticulously sorted, and nobody in this section to object to a modest withdrawal.

choices.text: Go deep, toward the sound

outcome_success.text: Four levels down you find the treasury — not gold; *metal*, worked and stockpiled over generations, the colony's entire strategic reserve. You take what two people can carry and navigate back out by the draught, and nothing ever knows you were there.

outcome_failure.text: You take a wrong branch and come out into a gallery that is not storage. The soldiers here are bigger.

choices.text: Announce yourself at the entrance and request an audience

outcome.text: You do it properly: stand at the threshold, state your names and your business, and wait. It takes three hours. Then a delegation comes up and conducts you down to trade, with an escort, through galleries no thief would ever have found. The colony deals fairly and at volume, and you leave through the front door.

animal_meadow_bhramara_hive.title: Bhramara Hive
animal_meadow_bhramara_hive.text:
The hive is built around a dead tree and has entirely replaced it — forty feet of grey papery architecture humming at a pitch you feel in your teeth.

There is a doorway. It is guarded, but it is unmistakably a doorway, which suggests visitors are a category that exists here.

choices.text: Admire it from a safe distance

outcome.text: The hum changes pitch as you withdraw. Acknowledgement, possibly. Or just weather.

choices.text: Trade at the doorway

outcome.text: The guards will not let you in, but they will exchange: your metal for their stores, at a rate they clearly consider generous and you cannot argue with because you cannot argue.

choices.text: Enter as the hive-mind's guest

outcome.text: You touch the wall and let the hum have you, and the distributed mind on the other side takes an interest. Inside there is no darkness — the whole structure glows faintly with worked wax — and the hive shows you its nurseries, its stores, its dead, with the unselfconsciousness of something that has never had a private thought in its existence. You come out three hours later, changed in a way that takes weeks to name.

choices.text: Whatever else this is, it is also the best food in the realm.

outcome.text:
It is. You trade properly for it rather than raiding, because you are greedy and not stupid, and you are given a comb still warm from the wall.

You make it last four days. Everyone else in the party gets some, eventually, after negotiation.

choices.text: Ask whether taking it costs the hive anything.

outcome.text:
Nobody asks. The hive-mind takes some time over the answer, which is itself interesting, and the answer is: some, but not much, and less than you would think, and thank you for asking.

You are given more than the traders get.

choices.text: Take from the outer stores at night

outcome_success.text: Cold night, slow hive, and a clean cut through the papery outer wall into a store gallery. You are away with a fortune in worked honey and wax before the temperature comes back up.

outcome_failure.text: The wall is not as cold as you judged, and the hum coming through it is rising.

animal_meadow_yaksha_standing_stones.title: Standing Stones
animal_meadow_yaksha_standing_stones.text:
Nine stones in a ring, each taller than a khadga, each carved with a face that has weathered to a suggestion. The grass inside the ring is a different species from the grass outside it.

The yaksha put these up. Nobody currently alive remembers why.

choices.text: Walk around the ring

outcome.text: You give it a wide berth, and are aware of doing so, and cannot entirely say why.

choices.text: Walk into the ring

outcome.text: It is markedly quieter inside. Not silent — quieter, as though the ring holds a slightly smaller amount of world. Nothing happens. You leave feeling that something declined to.

choices.text: Wake the ring

outcome.text: You put your hands on the northern stone and give it what it has been waiting a long time for. The nine faces do not move — they simply become, briefly, faces again, and the ring remembers that it is a ring. For about four heartbeats you are standing somewhere else, in a much older meadow, among a great many yaksha who are all looking at you with enormous surprise. Then it is a field with rocks in it.

choices.text: Nine stones. Count them again.

outcome.text:
You count them again. There are nine. You count a third time from the other direction and there are nine, and the fact that you needed to check three times is the thing worth paying attention to.

You make the offering at the one you kept losing.

choices.text: Work out what the ring was for

outcome.text: The stones are not aligned to the sun. They are aligned to each other, in a pattern that only makes sense if you assume a tenth stone that is no longer there. Something was held in this ring, by nine, and one of the nine failed. You do not find the tenth stone. You do find, at its position, a hollow where nothing will grow.

animal_meadow_patanga_cloud.title: Patanga Cloud
animal_meadow_patanga_cloud.text:
A column of patanga is rising off the warm ground in a slow spiral, thousands of them, catching the light — the whole thing perhaps two hundred feet high and turning like something being poured upward.

They are not going anywhere. This appears to be the entire activity.

choices.text: Walk on past

outcome.text: The column is still turning when you look back an hour later.

choices.text: Stop and watch it for a while

outcome.text: Twenty minutes of doing nothing at all, in good light, watching something beautiful that has no purpose. The party is measurably better afterwards.

choices.text: Walk through the column

outcome_success.text: Wings against every inch of exposed skin, light coming through in fragments, absolute disorientation for about ninety seconds. You come out the far side laughing and covered in scale-dust that will not brush off for a week.

outcome_failure.text: Somebody inhales. There follows a great deal of coughing, some panic, and an undignified exit at speed.

animal_meadow_khadga_herd.title: Khadga Herd
animal_meadow_khadga_herd.text: Forty khadga, grazing, spread across a mile of grassland directly across your route. Individually each one could end your afternoon. Collectively they are entirely occupied with eating and have not looked up.

choices.text: Go around — the long way

outcome.text: Four extra hours and total safety. Nobody complains, which tells you something about the party's opinion of khadga.

choices.text: Walk straight through at grazing pace

outcome_success.text: The trick, it turns out, is to move exactly as slowly as they do and never once change direction. It takes ninety minutes to cross a mile. Two calves follow you for part of it out of curiosity. Nothing else happens at all, which is a triumph.

outcome_failure.text: A bull on the flank decides he does not care for the shape of you and makes a short, emphatic demonstration run. Nobody is gored. Everybody runs. The crossing is abandoned.

choices.text: Forty animals and one of them is doing the watching.

outcome.text:
Second rank, north side, not grazing. Everything the herd will do in the next minute is already decided by her.

You plan the crossing around one animal instead of forty, and the herd never breaks.

choices.text: Walk in slowly. They will make room.

outcome.text:
They make room. It is not tameness — nothing here is tame — it is that you are moving at a speed that reads as weather rather than as threat.

The party follows in your wake, and the crossing takes an hour instead of a day.

choices.text: Something in that herd is not a khadga.

outcome.text:
Third group from the left, lying down, wrong shoulder line.

It has been in among them for some time and the herd has accepted it, which tells you considerably more about the thing than about the herd.

choices.text: Read the herd and cross behind the matriarchs

outcome.text: The old cows set the herd's mood, and they are downwind and settled. You cross in their lee, where the bulls take their cues from and therefore will not initiate anything, and are through in twenty minutes.

animal_meadow_migration.title: The Migration
animal_meadow_migration.text:
It has been passing for two days and shows no sign of ending: a river of bodies, twenty species deep, moving north across the entire visible width of the meadow. Predators walk in it openly, unmolested, because during the migration that is the arrangement.

You need to be on the other side.

choices.text: Camp and wait it out

outcome.text: Another day and a half. You spend it watching, and eat well — the migration sheds food the way a cart sheds straw.

choices.text: Cross through the flow

outcome_success.text: You go with the current at an angle, never against it, the way you would ford a river. Forty minutes inside a moving wall of animals that mostly ignore you. You come out a mile north of where you meant to and entirely intact.

outcome_failure.text: Somebody stumbles and the party fragments. You spend the rest of the day being carried north by a river of grazers and the following morning walking back south.

choices.text: It is going somewhere. That is the part that gets you.

outcome.text:
Two days of animals that know exactly where they are going and why, and will be there by a particular week, and have been doing it since before anyone was counting.

You watch a good deal more of it than the crossing requires.

choices.text: Walk with the migration as long as it goes your way

outcome.text: You match the pace and join it, and for six hours you are simply part of the thing, walking north among a hundred thousand animals under the truce. A shardula walks beside you for a mile. Neither of you acknowledges the other. It is, on later reflection, one of the great experiences of the run.

animal_meadow_grassfire.title: Grassfire
animal_meadow_grassfire.text:
The smoke line is on the southern horizon and it is wider than it was ten minutes ago. Grassfire moves faster than a running person when the wind is behind it, and the wind is behind it.

There is a rocky rise a mile east. There is a river two miles north. Neither is close enough to be comfortable.

choices.text: Run for the river

outcome.text: You make it, barely, and stand chest-deep watching a mile-wide front of fire go past on both banks. Somebody's pack is gone. Everybody's eyebrows are gone.

choices.text: Burn a firebreak and shelter in the black

outcome.text: You light your own fire downwind and let it eat a patch bare, then stand in the ash while the main front arrives and finds nothing to eat. It is loud, and hot, and completely survivable, and the party looks at whoever suggested it with new respect.

choices.text: Take the fire in hand

outcome.text: You do not put it out — it is a mile wide and older than your involvement. You persuade it to part. Two walls of flame go by on either side of a corridor thirty feet across, and for about four minutes the party walks through the middle of a grassfire in perfect safety and total terror.

choices.text: A fire front is a line. You have worked a line before.

outcome.text:
You stop the party from running, which is the entire job, and then you give four people four tasks in the order they need doing.

It is not courage. It is that panic is a thing you stopped being able to do some years ago, and it turns out to be worth more than courage here.

choices.text: There are animals in front of that fire.

outcome.text:
There are, and you are already moving toward them, and the argument about whether this is sensible happens behind you at volume.

You get perhaps a third of them out. The third is a real number of living things and you decline to be told otherwise.

choices.text: Drive the trapped grazers out ahead of the front

outcome.text: There is a pocket of young khadga penned against a gully and no time to do this and get clear yourself. You do it anyway, shouting and waving and running the gully line until they break the right way. You reach the river with the front close enough to read by. Later, in the meadow, khadga will not charge you. Word travels.

animal_meadow_thermal_column.title: Thermal Column
animal_meadow_thermal_column.text:
A bare patch of dark rock in the middle of the grass throws up heat all afternoon, and everything with wings in the meadow knows it. Shyena, kapota and uluka circle in a lazy stacked column half a mile high, none of them flapping, all of them going up.

At ground level it is simply a warm rock. It makes a good place to stop.

choices.text: Rest on the warm rock

outcome.text: An hour in the sun on hot stone with birds turning overhead. The party's aches ease and nobody says anything of consequence the entire time.

choices.text: Keep moving while the light holds

outcome.text: You make good distance. The column is still there behind you at dusk, thinning as the rock cools.

choices.text: Signal the birds down

outcome.text: You put a twist in the thermal — a stutter in the rising air that reads, to anything riding it, as an invitation. A kapota comes down to see what happened. She carries messages for a living, is intensely curious about ground-walkers, and trades you an hour of the meadow's news for the novelty of the conversation.

animal_meadow_merchant.title: Plains Merchant
animal_meadow_merchant.text:
The cart is enormous, the draught animal is a khadga in a padded harness, and the merchant is a yaksha who has clearly been doing this route for decades.

"Don't touch the wheels," she says by way of greeting. "Everything else is negotiable."

choices.text: See what she carries

outcome.text: The cart opens out into a shop-front with practiced efficiency.

choices.text: Move on

outcome.text: "Suit yourself. I'll be at the standing stones in four days if you change your mind."

choices.text: Haggle properly

outcome.text: Forty minutes of extremely enjoyable commerce. She opens by insulting your boots; you close by pointing out that her khadga is favouring a foreleg and she is four days from anyone who can shoe it. You both leave delighted. Your prices are excellent.

choices.text: Offer to see to the khadga's foreleg

outcome.text: There is a stone bruise under the plate and the beginnings of an abscess. You open it, drain it, pack it, and explain the aftercare twice. The merchant watches the whole thing without a word, then loads your packs with whatever you point at and refuses money. "That animal is my business," she says. "You just saved my business."
